slides.direction: Draw the commit object first, line by line, as `git cat-file -p` prints it. Then box the `gpgsig` header. Then draw the bracket over everything else, and say: these are the bytes handed to the signing program.
slides.text:
the commit object, as stored
   +--------------------------------------------------+
   | tree      <tree ID>                              | --+
   | parent    <parent ID>                            |   |
   | author    name <email> date                      |   |  signed bytes:
   | committer name <email> date                      |   |  the object WITHOUT gpgsig
   +--------------------------------------------------+   |
   | gpgsig -----BEGIN SSH SIGNATURE-----             |   |
   |  (continuation lines start with a space)         |   |  <- the signature itself
   |  -----END SSH SIGNATURE-----                     |   |     is not among them
   +--------------------------------------------------+   |
   |                                                  |   |
   | message                                          | --+
   +--------------------------------------------------+
        the whole object, signature included, is hashed  ->  commit ID

slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 14B.16, one line at a time. Observed behavior: `git log --show-signature` prints "No signature", and `%G?` prints N, for a commit that visibly has a gpgsig header. Git state: the commit is signed; `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile` is not set. Mechanism: SSH verification means "find this key in my list of allowed signers"; without a list Git does not start ssh-keygen at all and reports no result. Root cause: signing needs one key; verifying needs a statement of whom you trust. Why Git does this: an SSH key has no owner written into it and no web of trust; the manual says trust is "fully" when the key is in the file and "undefined" otherwise. Correct fix: create the allowed-signers file and point `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile` at it. Prevention: distribute the file with the signing setup; a team can keep it in the repository.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : git log --show-signature prints "No signature", and %G? prints N, for a
                    commit that visibly has a gpgsig header.
Git state         : the commit is signed. gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile is not set.
Mechanism         : SSH verification means "find this key in my list of allowed signers".
                    Without a list Git does not start ssh-keygen at all and reports no result.
Root cause        : signing needs one key; verifying needs a statement of whom you trust.
Why Git does this : an SSH key has no owner written into it and no web of trust. The manual:
                    trust is "fully" when the key is in the file and "undefined" otherwise.
Correct fix       : create the allowed-signers file and point gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile at it.
Prevention        : distribute the file with the signing setup; a team can keep it in the repository.

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: A signature covers the bytes of one commit or tag without the signature, and is stored inside the object: the gpgsig header in a commit, a block after the message in a tag.
Git does no cryptography; gpg.format selects gpg, gpgsm or ssh-keygen.
SSH signing needs gpg.format, user.signingKey and, for verification, gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile.
Without an allowed-signers file, a signed commit reports "No signature".
A good signature is a fact about a key; a trusted signer is your decision about that key.

Without an allowed-signers file, a signed commit reports "No signature".
A good signature is a fact about a key; a trusted signer is your decision about that key.

beats.text: In one sentence. A Git signature is a detached cryptographic signature over the bytes of one commit or one annotated tag, produced by an external program and stored inside that object.
beats.tele: In one sentence. A Git signature is a detached cryptographic signature over the bytes of one commit or one annotated tag, produced by an external program and stored inside that object.

beats.text: Precisely. Git computes the object without a signature, hands those bytes to a signing program, and embeds the result. In a commit the result is the gpgsig header. In a tag it is a block appended to the message. That means an annotated tag, which is an object of its own. Since the signature is part of the object, it's covered by the object ID, the hash that names the object.
beats.tele: Precisely. Git computes the object without a signature, hands those bytes to a signing program, and embeds the result. In a commit the result is the `gpgsig` header. In a tag it is a block appended to the message. That means an annotated tag, which is an object of its own. Since the signature is part of the object, it's covered by the object ID, the hash that names the object.

beats.text: Don't confuse two options that differ only in the case of one letter. Capital -S signs with a key. Lower-case -s adds the Signed-off-by text to the message. One is cryptography. The other is a line of text anyone can type.

beats.text: Which program. The setting gpg.format chooses.
beats.tele: Which program. The setting `gpg.format` chooses.

beats.text: With openpgp, the default, the program is gpg. The key is chosen by user.signingKey, or else by the committer identity. Trust is decided by your GnuPG keyring and its trust levels.

beats.text: With x509, available since Git 2.19, the program is gpgsm. The key is chosen the same way, and trust is decided by the certificate chain.
beats.tele: With `x509`, available since Git 2.19, the program is `gpgsm`. The key is chosen the same way, and trust is decided by the certificate chain.

beats.text: With ssh, available since Git 2.34, the program is ssh-keygen. The key is user.signingKey, which is a key file, or a literal key with an agent, or else the command in gpg.ssh.defaultKeyCommand. And trust is decided by one plain text file: the file named by gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile.

beats.text: The rest of the course uses SSH signing, for two reasons the textbook gives: you already have SSH keys, and the trust file is plain text. OpenPGP and X.509 signing aren't run in the labs, because both would start an agent process.

beats.text: Signing and verifying need different things. This is the idea that the whole second half of the demonstration rests on. Signing needs one key. Verifying needs a statement of whom you trust. An SSH key has no owner written into it and there's no web of trust. So with SSH, verification means: find this key in my list of allowed signers. Without a list, Git doesn't start ssh-keygen at all.
beats.tele: Signing and verifying need different things. This is the idea that the whole second half of the demonstration rests on. Signing needs one key. Verifying needs a statement of whom you trust. An SSH key has no owner written into it and there's no web of trust. So with SSH, verification means: find this key in my list of allowed signers. Without a list, Git doesn't start `ssh-keygen` at all.

beats.text: An allowed-signers line has three parts. First a principal, which by convention is an email address. Then optional options. Then a public key. The option namespaces="git" restricts the key to Git signatures.

beats.text: The result letters. For scripts, the format placeholder %G? gives one letter. G is a good signature: the key is in the allowed-signers file and valid at the signature's time. B is a bad signature: the object was altered after signing, or the key is listed in the revocation file.
beats.tele: The result letters. For scripts, the format placeholder `%G?` gives one letter. `G` is a good signature: the key is in the allowed-signers file and valid at the signature's time. `B` is a bad signature: the object was altered after signing, or the key is listed in the revocation file.

beats.text: U is a good signature with unknown validity: the key isn't in the file, or outside its validity window. N is no signature, and it's also printed, with an error, when no allowed-signers file is configured. The manual lists X, Y, R and E as well. The SSH demos of the chapter don't produce them.

beats.text: Analogy. A seal pressed onto one page of a ledger. Because each page cites earlier pages by numbers computed from their content, the seal vouches for the whole history behind it.
beats.tele: Analogy. A seal pressed onto one page of a ledger. Because each page cites earlier pages by numbers computed from their content, the seal vouches for the whole history behind it.

beats.text: Follow that through. The signed bytes include the tree ID, so the seal covers every file. They include the parent IDs, so the seal covers every ancestor. One signature on the newest commit vouches for the content of everything it is built on.
beats.tele: Follow that through. The signed bytes include the tree ID, so the seal covers every file. They include the parent IDs, so the seal covers every ancestor. One signature on the newest commit vouches for the content of everything it is built on.

beats.text: The analogy breaks where it matters most, and the textbook says so in one sentence: the seal says which ring was used, not whose hand held it. A signature is evidence about a key. Whether that key was in the hand of the person named in the author line is a different question, and no cryptography answers it.

beats.tele: A signature covers the bytes of one commit or tag without the signature, and is stored inside the object: the `gpgsig` header in a commit, a block after the message in a tag.

beats.text: Git does no cryptography; gpg.format selects gpg, gpgsm or ssh-keygen.
beats.tele: Git does no cryptography; `gpg.format` selects `gpg`, `gpgsm` or `ssh-keygen`.

beats.text: SSH signing needs gpg.format, user.signingKey and, for verification, gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile.
beats.tele: SSH signing needs `gpg.format`, `user.signingKey` and, for verification, `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile`.

beats.text: Without an allowed-signers file, a signed commit reports "No signature".
beats.tele: Without an allowed-signers file, a signed commit reports "No signature".

beats.text: A good signature is a fact about a key; a trusted signer is your decision about that key.
beats.tele: A good signature is a fact about a key; a trusted signer is your decision about that key.

beats.text: Today you signed a commit and a tag, and you watched "No signature" become a good signature by adding one line of trust. Practise on a repository of yours before the next video. Next time: what a signature covers, what verification proves, and author spoofing. Until then, look at the state first and type second. See you in the next one.
